messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] measurement error and landmark averaging
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

This turned out to be an issue with arrayspecs  (actually a base R function used in arrayspecs), which is called by coords.subset, specifically with assigning names to subsetted objects.  I was able to add a patch, and now the update can be found on Github.  Unfortunately, we just launched an updated R version on CRAN, so this patch comes in just a little too late to be current with the CRAN version of R.  You can update your version of geomorph with

devtools::install_github(“geomorphR/geomorph”, ref = “Stable”)

You might also have to update RRPP, if you have not already installed geomorph, 3.0.7

devtools::install_github(“mlcollyer/RRPP”)

Sorry about the hassle but thanks for discovering the issue!

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Nick,

simplfy2array will attempt to turn a list into an array.  However, I’m not sure what you are requesting.  If you use coords.subset with a factor for specimen, you have a list of arrays of coordinates, by specimen.  If you are asking if you can have arrays within arrays, the answer to that is also yes, provided everything is balanced.  4D, 5D, etc., arrays are possible.  You can create them from a list using the array function.  Good luck making sense of them, though!

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
I find the str function in R to be kind of clunky.  Sometimes it seems to retain the original properties of objects that have been manipulated.  Within coords.subset, first data are sorted into a data.frame and split by groups.  This produces a list.  Within the list objects (group levels) the data are reformatted into arrays.  Apparently, the str function wants to believe that in the process of reformatting - where lists are created and converted to arrays - that the output retains the properties of lists.  I can assure you that the output is a list of arrays, even if str sees it as a lists of lists.  For example,

> data(pupfish)
> group <- factor(paste(pupfish$Pop, pupfish$Sex))
> levels(group)
[1] "Marsh F"    "Marsh M"    "Sinkhole F" "Sinkhole M"
> new.coords <- coords.subset(A = pupfish$coords, group = group)
> sapply(new.coords, class)
   Marsh F    Marsh M Sinkhole F Sinkhole M
   "array"    "array"    "array"    "array"
> sapply(new.coords, is.array)
   Marsh F    Marsh M Sinkhole F Sinkhole M
      TRUE       TRUE       TRUE       TRUE
> str(new.coords$`Marsh M`)
List of 1456
 $ : num -0.0352
 $ : num -0.0361
 $ : num 0.0911

So, R can see that arrays were produced, but str wishes to say they have a different structure.  I don’t know why str does this, but I believe the issue is with the str function rather than coords.subset.

Mike

messages.subject: Scaling issue in 3D models
messages.body_plain:
Dear list, I’m conducting a 3D GM on small mandibles with geomorph. I’m not used to work in 3D so my knowledge about meshes and 3D models is limited. All models are from microCT scanning except two, that are from a laser scanner. One problem that I’m facing is that despite the landmarks coordinates are multiplied by the scale factor, the two model from the laser scanner have an extremely low centroid size, compared with the rest of the sample. Moreover, this "size" difference do not really exists since this two specimens with a very small centroid sizes, have an average real size. The 3d landmarks are acquired with IDAV Landmark editor, saved in nts format. The scaling procedure is carried out in R,  following a modified code from geomorph 3 quick guide:

vec_scale # Vector of real distance in mm between landmarks 4 and 5 for each specimen
for (i in 1:dim(coords)[3]){
scb <- coords[4:5,,i]
scale <- sqrt((scb[1,1]-scb[2,1])^2+(scb[1,2]-scb[2,2])^2+(scb[1,3]-scb[2,3])^2)/vec_scale[i]
coords[,,i] <- coords[,,i]*scale }
coords <- coords[-(4:5),,] # remove the landmarks 4 and 5

The reason way I’m scaling in R and not in Landmark editor is that Landmark editor always save my coordinates without calibration, no matter if I check “Use calibrated coordinates based on...” when exporting the landmark coordinates.
I really don't know if I missing something in the scaling procedure or the issue is the difference in the source resolution of the models. Any tips will be very appreciated!.

Kind regards,

Ale

Seán,

The simplest way to do bootstrap resampling is with the sample function in R, using an important argument, replace = FALSE.

For any array of shapes, there are three dimensions.  For example

dim(A)

produces three numbers in the order of p, k, n.  If you want to sample specimens, try this:

spec.ind <- 1 : (dim(A)[3])
sample(spec.ind, replace = FALSE) # finds a random sampling of 1 to n, with replacement

A[, , sample(spec.ind, replace = FALSE) ] # finds a random sampling of 1 to n, with replacement, and selects their landmarks from A

If you want to sample landmarks, try this

lm.ind <- 1 : (dim(A)[1])
sample(lm.ind, replace = FALSE) # finds a random sampling of 1 to p, with replacement

A[sample(lm.ind, replace = FALSE), , ] # finds a random sampling of 1 to p, with replacement, and selects those points from A

In a loop, one would do something like the following:

SSD <- list()
pers <- 999

for(i in 1:perms) {

# calculate statistics using bootstrap permutations, as above and your math
SSD[[i]] <- stat or c(stat1, stat2, …)
}

I used 999, in case you want to append the observed case to the list to make it 1,000.  Thus,

SSD <- c(obs, SSD)

would do that.

Hope that helps!
Mike

In the paper that you cite, on the Brachyrhine mouse (Willmore et al 2006), we used FA 10 as the metric for the population, for the reason given—it takes measurement error into account.  To answer the more general question that you’re asking about the relationship between metrics for individual FA and population-level metrics, two papers that thoroughly review that subject are Palmer and Strobeck 1986, and Palmer and Strobeck 2003.  There is another paper that proposes a metric for FA more specific to analyses of geometric morphometric data, Klingenberg and Monteiro, 2005.  If you plan to use the deviations of each individual from the symmetric mean, taking directional asymmetry into account, you can derive that from the FA.component returned by geomorph. As the manual says, that is the specimen-specific side deviation, adjusted for the mean directional asymmetry.  The answer to your last question, on how to obtain the two-way mixed model ANOVA from geomorph, should be more obvious now that the mislabeling of the terms in the table returned by the bilat.symmetry function is corrected.  However, it sounds like you had only two factors in your model, ind and sides, i.e., you did not specify the replicates.  If you do have replicates, you should include that factor in your geomorph dataframe and in the argument for the function, following the first example in the manual.
Willmore, K. E., M. L. Zelditch, N. Young, A. Ah-Seng, S. Lozanoff, and B. Hallgrimsson. 2006. Canalization and developmental stability in the Brachyrrhine mouse. Journal of Anatomy 208:361-372.
Klingenberg, C. P. and L. R. Monteiro. 2005. Distances and directions in multidimensional shape spaces: Implications for morphometric applications. Syst. Biol. 54:678-688.
Palmer, A.R. and C. Strobeck. 1986. Fluctuating asymmetry: measurement, analysis, patterns. Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 17: 391–421.
Palmer, A. R and C. Strobeck. 2003. Fluctuating Asymmetry Analysis Unplugged. In: Developmental Instability (DI): Causes and Consequences (ed. Polak M), pp. 279–319. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

messages.body_plain:
Sean

One other thing I would add on top of what Mike has already suggested is that it may be worth spending a bit of time learning how to use the boot library. While a simple non-parametric bootstrap is very easy to write thanks to indexing and the sample function, there are a few aspects that are incredibly helpful which the boot library makes efficient. In particular the "strata" argument (so you can sample with replacement within each level of a treatment group, i.e. sampling within male observations and within female observations, but keeping their sample sizes the same as in the real data set). Additionally, getting slightly "better" approximations of the confidence intervals (like the bias corrected and accelerated, BCa confidence intervals) is an important plus. These can also be coded by hand, and are not that difficult, but the boot library has been "checked" by many eyes and so there is less chance of little goofy errors.

Also, there are some nice tutorials available for bootstrapping (using R). Keep in mind though that since for each observation your response vector is multidimensional, to sample using the index and not the observations themselves.

A great one is
https://socialsciences.mcmaster.ca/jfox/Books/Companion/appendix/Appendix-Bootstrapping.pdf

Here is one of my old tutorials. Not a great set, but they may be useful
 https://youtu.be/TP6r5CTd9yM

Cheers
Ian

Yes that can be a bit persnickety. What is happening here is that you are selecting a point on the surface that has no data (recall a surface is a cloud of points, but it is represented as a mesh of polygons in-between them). Zooming in more on the location on the surface can often help with this.
